modules.title: Environment and society
modules.summary: Climate, cities and public services: hypothesise about the past, express regret and propose solutions.
modules.vocabularyTopic: Climate, sustainability, cities and public services

grammar.name: Third and mixed conditionals
grammar.explanation: The third conditional imagines an unreal past; mixed conditionals connect an unreal past to a present result, or a present state to a past result.
keyPoints: Third: If the city had invested earlier, the floods would not have been so severe.
Past → present: If I had studied planning, I would be working on this project now.
Present → past: If she were more patient, she would not have quit.
grammar.example: If the council had built the drainage in 2015, the damage would not be costing us millions now.

items.prompt: If the city had invested earlier, the floods ___ so severe.
items.explanation: Third conditional: had + past participle, would have + past participle.

items.prompt: If I had studied planning, I ___ on this project now.
items.explanation: Mixed conditional: past cause with a present result.

items.prompt: Which sentence blames a past action for a present situation?
options: If we had acted, the park would be open now.
If we act, the park will open.
If we were acting, the park would be open.
items.answer: If we had acted, the park would be open now.
items.explanation: Past perfect in the if-clause plus present result is the mixed pattern.

grammar.name: Wish, if only and regret structures
grammar.explanation: Use wish or if only with the past simple for a present regret, with the past perfect for a past regret, and with would to complain about someone else's behaviour.
keyPoints: Present regret: I wish I lived closer to work.
Past regret: I wish we had started ten years ago.
Complaint: I wish the council would collect the bins on time.
grammar.example: I wish the city had kept the old tram line; if only we could use it now.

items.prompt: I wish I ___ closer to work.
items.explanation: A present regret takes the past simple after wish.

items.prompt: I wish we ___ ten years ago.
items.explanation: A past regret takes the past perfect after wish.

items.prompt: Which sentence complains about someone else's behaviour?
options: I wish I had a bike.
I wish the council would fix the road.
items.answer: I wish the council would fix the road.
items.explanation: Wish + would expresses irritation about another person's action.

inputs.title: Documentary excerpt: the city that cooled itself
inputs.body: In 2019 this square was a car park. Summer temperatures here were four degrees higher than in the park two streets away, an effect researchers call the urban heat island. The city tried something unfashionable: it planted trees, removed the asphalt and put a small fountain where the delivery vans used to park. Four years later, the temperature difference has almost disappeared. The scheme cost less than one kilometre of road. What surprised the engineers was not the cooling, but how quickly residents started using the space.

options: How quickly residents used the space
questions.answer: How quickly residents used the space

inputs.title: Problem, solution: the heat in our streets
inputs.body: Cities are hotter than the countryside around them, and the difference is not evenly spread. Districts with fewer trees and more asphalt can be five degrees warmer than wealthier, greener neighbours, which means the people least able to afford air conditioning are the ones who need it most. The solutions are unglamorous and well understood: plant mature trees rather than saplings, replace dark surfaces with reflective ones, and open air-conditioned public buildings during heatwaves. The obstacle is rarely knowledge. It is the budget cycle, which rewards visible new projects over invisible maintenance.

questions.prompt: Who suffers most from urban heat?
options: Districts with fewer trees and less money
questions.answer: Districts with fewer trees and less money

questions.prompt: What does the writer say is the real obstacle?

speaking.title: Propose a solution to a local problem
speaking.prompt: Identify one environmental problem in your area and propose a realistic solution. Explain the cost, the benefit and the obstacle. Two minutes.
phrases: The problem in my area is...

speaking.title: Role-play: the council meeting
speaking.prompt: You are presenting a proposal to close a street to traffic. A resident objects. Present the plan, respond to the objection and negotiate one compromise. Two minutes.

speaking.title: Shadowing: hypothetical past
speaking.prompt: Shadow the clip, keeping the weak forms in would have and had been clear.
phrases: If the council / had acted sooner, / we wouldn't have lost / the square.

writing.title: Problem-solution report: a local issue
writing.prompt: Write a 180–200-word report for a residents' association about one local environmental problem. Describe the problem, analyse two causes, propose two solutions and recommend one.

outline.analyze: Purpose: inform and recommend. Audience: residents and local officials. Register: formal, impersonal.
outline.draft: Use the passive, one third or mixed conditional, and linkers of cause and consequence.
outline.improve: Replace informal phrasing with impersonal constructions; add figures or comparisons.
outline.review: Check that each solution answers one of the causes you described.

lessons.title: Third conditional: the past we did not have
lessons.objective: Imagine alternative past outcomes and their consequences.
lessons.canDo: I can discuss how a past decision could have produced a different result.
lessons.output: Record five third-conditional sentences about a decision your city or company made.

lessons.title: Mixed conditionals: past cause, present result
lessons.objective: Connect an unreal past to a present situation and vice versa.
lessons.canDo: I can link a past decision to a present consequence in one sentence.
lessons.output: Record four mixed conditionals about the environment or your own life.

lessons.title: Wish and if only: expressing regret
lessons.objective: Express present and past regrets and complaints with the right structure.
lessons.canDo: I can express regret about the past and irritation about the present.
lessons.output: Record five sentences with wish and if only about your city or your studies.

lessons.title: Vocabulary: environment and cities
lessons.objective: Discuss climate and urban issues with ten precise expressions.
lessons.canDo: I can describe environmental and urban problems with topic vocabulary.
lessons.output: Record 60 seconds describing your area using six new expressions.

lessons.title: Listening: the city that cooled itself
lessons.objective: Follow a documentary extract and catch cause, effect and evaluation.
lessons.canDo: I can follow a documentary extract and separate facts from the speaker's evaluation.
lessons.output: Note three facts and one evaluation from the documentary extract.

lessons.title: Reading: the heat in our streets
lessons.objective: Map a problem-solution text: problem, causes, solutions, obstacle.
lessons.canDo: I can read a problem-solution article and reconstruct its argument structure.
lessons.output: Write the problem, two causes, two solutions and the obstacle in the article.

lessons.title: Speaking: proposing a solution
lessons.objective: Present a proposal with cost, benefit and obstacle in two minutes.
lessons.canDo: I can propose a realistic solution and anticipate the main objection.
lessons.output: Use the prompt card: problem, solution, cost, obstacle.

lessons.title: Writing: problem-solution report
lessons.objective: Write a structured formal report of 180–200 words.
lessons.canDo: I can write a formal problem-solution report with causes, solutions and a recommendation.
lessons.output: Draft, then edit for impersonal register and clear cause-effect links.

modules.title: Health and ethics
modules.summary: Lifestyle, choice and responsibility: arrange services, weigh arguments and write a formal essay.
modules.vocabularyTopic: Health, lifestyle, ethics and consumer choices

grammar.name: Causatives: have / get something done
grammar.explanation: Use have or get something done when someone else performs a service for you, and have someone do something when you arrange it directly.
keyPoints: Service: I had my blood pressure checked last week.
Arrangement: She got the pharmacy to deliver the prescription.
Trouble: He had his appendix removed on Monday.
grammar.example: I had my eyes tested on Friday and got the optician to adjust the lenses for free.

items.prompt: I ___ my blood pressure checked last week.
items.explanation: Have + object + past participle shows a service performed by someone else.

items.prompt: Which sentence means someone else did the work?
items.explanation: The causative makes the agent of the action someone other than the subject.

items.prompt: She ___ the pharmacy to deliver the prescription.
items.explanation: Get + person + to + infinitive describes persuading or arranging.

grammar.name: Advanced linkers: whereas, consequently, nevertheless, in spite of
grammar.explanation: Advanced writing needs linkers that signal contrast, consequence and concession precisely, with the right grammar after each one.
keyPoints: Contrast between clauses: Whereas the tax raised revenue, it hit low earners hardest.
Consequence: Consequently, consumption fell by eighteen per cent.
Concession: Nevertheless, the measure remains controversial. / In spite of the criticism, it stayed.
grammar.example: Whereas the levy reduced consumption, it was criticised as regressive; nevertheless, the government has kept it, in spite of two legal challenges.

items.prompt: ___ the tax raised revenue, it hit low earners hardest.
items.explanation: Whereas introduces a direct contrast between two clauses.

items.prompt: Consumption fell sharply; ___, revenue also dropped.
items.explanation: Consequently marks a result of the previous statement.

items.prompt: ___ the criticism, the policy remained in place.
items.explanation: In spite of + noun phrase expresses concession.

vocab.example: A balanced diet matters more than any single superfood.

vocab.definition: a way of living with very little physical activity
vocab.example: A sedentary lifestyle raises the risk of heart disease.

vocab.definition: the state of feeling psychologically healthy
vocab.example: Sleep affects mental wellbeing more than most people realise.

vocab.example: I am cutting down on sugary drinks.

vocab.definition: difficult to stop doing or consuming
vocab.example: Highly processed food is designed to be addictive.

vocab.definition: morally right or acceptable
vocab.example: Is it ethical to advertise junk food to children?

vocab.definition: trade that pays producers a fair price
vocab.example: The café only sells fair trade coffee.

vocab.example: Several cities now tax sugary drinks.

vocab.definition: the health of a whole population, and the policy around it

inputs.title: Should junk food be taxed? Two views
inputs.body: FOR: The case is straightforward. Sugar taxes reduce consumption, and consumption of sugar raises the risk of diseases that cost public health systems billions. A levy of ten per cent in one European country cut purchases of sugary drinks by eighteen per cent within a year, and the revenue funded free school meals. AGAINST: The case is equally straightforward. Such taxes are regressive: they take a larger share of income from poorer households, who also have less time to cook and fewer affordable alternatives. Education and better labelling would achieve more, and would not punish people for buying what is cheapest.

options: An eighteen per cent drop in purchases
questions.answer: An eighteen per cent drop in purchases

inputs.title: Panel discussion: whose responsibility is health?
inputs.body: CHAIR: Whose responsibility is health? DR OSEI: I get uncomfortable when we talk only about individual choice, because choice is shaped. If the only shop within a kilometre sells processed food, that is not a free choice. DR LEWIS: I agree up to a point, but people do respond to information. Smoking fell for decades before any ban, largely because attitudes changed. CHAIR: So is taxation part of the answer? DR OSEI: It can be, provided the revenue goes back into prevention. Otherwise it just looks like a fine on being poor.

questions.prompt: Why does Dr Osei distrust the 'individual choice' argument?
options: Because choice is shaped by the environment
questions.answer: Because choice is shaped by the environment

questions.prompt: What condition does Dr Osei set for taxation?
options: It must apply only to the rich

speaking.title: Debate: should junk food be taxed?
speaking.prompt: Argue either for or against a tax on junk food. Use two pieces of evidence, address the strongest objection and conclude. Two to three minutes.

speaking.title: Role-play: the doctor's appointment
speaking.prompt: You are explaining a change in your lifestyle to a doctor. Describe your habits, ask about two treatments, and agree on one plan. Two minutes.

speaking.title: Shadowing: concession and consequence
speaking.prompt: Shadow the clip, marking the pause after Nevertheless and the stress on Whereas.
phrases: Whereas the tax raised revenue, / it hit low earners hardest. / Nevertheless, / it stayed.

writing.title: Argument essay: health and responsibility
writing.prompt: Write a 200-word argument essay: should governments tax unhealthy products to improve public health? Present both sides and reach a clear conclusion.

outline.analyze: Purpose: argue and conclude. Audience: an examiner or opinion page. Register: formal.
outline.plan: Introduction with position → argument for → argument against → evaluation → conclusion.
outline.draft: Use at least three advanced linkers and one causative structure.
outline.improve: Qualify your claims; replace absolutes with hedging where evidence is limited.
outline.review: Check that the conclusion follows from the evaluation, not from repetition.

lessons.title: Causatives: have and get something done
lessons.objective: Describe services and arrangements with have/get + object + past participle.
lessons.canDo: I can talk about services I arrange for other people to do.
lessons.output: Record five sentences about services you have had done this year.

lessons.title: Linkers of contrast and consequence
lessons.objective: Use whereas, consequently and related linkers with correct punctuation and grammar.
lessons.canDo: I can contrast two ideas and state a consequence precisely in writing.
lessons.output: Write four sentences contrasting two habits or policies, using whereas and consequently.

lessons.title: Linkers of concession: nevertheless, in spite of
lessons.objective: Concede a point without weakening your argument.
lessons.canDo: I can concede a valid objection and still defend my position.
lessons.output: Record four sentences that concede a point and then defend a position.

lessons.title: Vocabulary: health and ethics
lessons.objective: Discuss lifestyle, choice and responsibility with ten precise expressions.
lessons.canDo: I can discuss health and consumer ethics using topic vocabulary accurately.
lessons.output: Record 60 seconds on one health habit you would change, using five new expressions.

lessons.title: Reading: should junk food be taxed?
lessons.objective: Compare two opposed arguments and identify the evidence used by each.
lessons.canDo: I can read two opposing arguments and summarise the evidence on both sides.
lessons.output: Write two columns: the strongest point and the weakest point of each side.

lessons.title: Listening: whose responsibility is health?
lessons.objective: Follow a panel discussion and track who holds which position.
lessons.canDo: I can follow a panel discussion and identify each speaker's position and condition.
lessons.output: Note each speaker's position in one sentence, plus one condition they set.

lessons.title: Speaking: the junk food debate
lessons.objective: Argue a contested position, handle the strongest objection and conclude.
lessons.canDo: I can debate a public health question for two to three minutes with evidence and concession.
lessons.output: Use the prompt card: position, evidence, objection, conclusion.

lessons.title: Writing: argument essay
lessons.objective: Plan and write a balanced 200-word essay with a reasoned conclusion.
lessons.canDo: I can write a 200-word argument essay that evaluates both sides and concludes clearly.
lessons.output: Draft, then edit for hedging and linkers.
